records.name_note: NC State's Common Name(s) field lists four entries — Buckeye, Fetid Buckeye, Horse Chestnut, Ohio Buckeye — alphabetized, in the same order as its page-title parenthetical. NC State's description opens "Ohio buckeye is a low-branched, small to medium-sized deciduous tree in the soapberry family (Sapindaceae)", MoBot's Common Name field reads "Ohio buckeye", and RHS's plant-profile subtitle beneath the H1 reads "Ohio buckeye", so that name is used here. Fetid buckeye is a secondary alias: NC State says "The flowers, bark, and stems, have an unpleasant odor when crushed, hence the sometimes common name of fetid buckeye", and MoBot says "All parts of this tree, particularly the flowers, bark and twigs, emit an unpleasant odor when bruised, hence the sometimes common name of fetid buckeye."
records.toxicity_detail: NC State carries a Poison block for this species (Plant Type includes "Poisonous"). Its Poison Severity is Low -- this rating is human-scoped, from NC State's Poison heading, and is separate from its Problem-for-Cats/Problem-for-Dogs tags. Poison Part field (three separate entries): Fruits, Leaves, Stems. Poison Symptoms (full list): "Muscle weakness and paralysis, dilated pupils, vomiting, diarrhea, depression, paralysis, and stupor". Toxic principle: "Glycoside aesculin, saponin aescin, possibly alkaloids". NC State's Problems tags, listed alongside the Poison block, are: Messy, Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses, Weedy -- the horse-scoped tag is disclosed here but is not used to support toxic_to_pets, which is confirmed instead by the Problem for Cats and Problem for Dogs tags. RHS separately corroborates cat/dog-adjacent risk with a dog-scoped notice: "Humans/Pets (dogs): harmful if eaten," and adds a handling warning: "Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling." NC State's description separately states "The seeds, leaves and bark are poisonous." -- the structured Poison Part field lists Fruits, Leaves and Stems while the description also names seeds and bark, a within-source difference on which parts are hazardous, reported here rather than resolved. The Poison block also carries Causes Contact Dermatitis: No. RHS's "Potentially harmful" field continues past the handling warning quoted above with a referral: "For further information and contact numbers regarding pets, see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants".
unknowns: soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are left null: NC State has no Soil pH field for this species, and RHS's soil pH field lists both acid and alkaline soils as acceptable ("Acid or Alkaline or Neutral"), so neither a floor nor a ceiling is supported.

water_regime is left null: the only structured moisture field found is MoBot's "Water: Medium", which per the schema's rules is mid-scale and cannot support keep_moist or any other regime token on its own; no species-specific watering statement was found.

part_sun and full_shade were excluded from outdoor_sun_exposure: none of NC State's Light field, MoBot's Sun field, or RHS's Position field state either value for this species; all three agree on full sun and partial shade only.

records.name_note: MoBot and RHS both lead with 'red buckeye' — MoBot's Common Name field carries the single value 'red buckeye', and RHS's page title and plant-profile subtitle are 'Aesculus pavia | red buckeye' / 'red buckeye'. NC State's Common Name(s) list is alphabetized (Firecracker Plant, Red Buckeye, Scarlet Buckeye), matching its page-title parenthetical, and marks no primary; its description prose opens with 'Red buckeye.' 'Firecracker Plant,' 'Scarlet Buckeye,' and RHS's 'red horse chestnut' (listed under Other common names) are secondary names.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Poison block (headed "Poisonous to Humans," so this severity/symptom data is human-scoped) rates Poison Severity as High, states the toxic principle as "Glycoside aesculin, saponin aescin, possibly alkaloids," and gives symptoms as "Poisonous if ingested. Highly toxic, may be fatal if eaten. Symptoms may include muscle weakness and paralysis, dilated pupils, vomiting, diarrhea, depression, paralysis, and stupor." Causes Contact Dermatitis is listed as "No." The full Poison Part list is Bark, Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Seeds, and Stems — every plant part is implicated, not just seeds or leaves. Separately from this human-scoped Poison block, NC State's structured Problem tags list this plant as a "Problem for Cats," "Problem for Dogs," and "Problem for Horses" (in addition to "Poisonous to Humans"), extending toxicity concern to cats and dogs specifically even though no separate cat/dog symptom list is given. RHS adds its own pet-specific note naming dogs directly: "Humans/Pets (dogs): harmful if eaten," and includes a handling warning not present on the NC State page: "Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling." No admissible source restricts toxicity to only one plant part or disputes the High/harmful rating; none give a distinct cat- or dog-specific symptom list beyond the tag/label naming them as at risk.
unknowns: direct_sun_hours_max left null: NC State's '2-6 hours' figure appears only inside its site-wide Light-category legend text ("Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)"), not in species-specific prose, so per the sourcing rule it is not usable as this plant's specific max-hours figure.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State's Soil pH field reads 'Neutral (6.0-8.0),' a closed band that would otherwise set a 6.0 floor and 8.0 ceiling, but RHS's pH field for this species lists 'Acid or Alkaline or Neutral' — RHS explicitly accepts both acid and alkaline soils, so both the floor and ceiling are disclosed as unsupported and left null per the cross-check rule.

water_regime left null: no admissible source gives a species-specific watering statement or dry-down instruction. MoBot's structured Water field reads 'Medium,' which is mid-scale and, per rule, cannot on its own support keep_moist or any other regime token; it is noted here only as a disclosed, unused data point.

humidity_need, humidity_pct_min/max, light_fc_min/good, chill_damage_f, cool_rest_note, day/night temperature fields, water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing/dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis, and all fertilize_* fields left null: no admissible source (NC State, MoBot, RHS) states any of these for Aesculus pavia specifically; this is an in-ground landscape shrub/tree, so per rule the day-interval and dry-down-target watering fields are left null by default absent a source framing watering that way.

Toxic principle and poison severity are stated only for oral ingestion (human-scoped) by NC State; no admissible source gives a distinct dose, LD50, or cat/dog-specific clinical course beyond naming cats and dogs as 'Problem for' categories.

Sources used: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox (plants.ces.ncsu.edu), Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder (plantfinder.mobot.org), and RHS Plants (rhs.org.uk) — all confirmed as species-specific pages for Aesculus pavia (RHS page verified by URL slug 'aesculus-pavia' and exact page title 'Aesculus pavia | red buckeye' before use). Clemson, UGA fieldreport, UF/IFAS, Penn State, and UMD extension sites did not return an admissible dedicated page for this species during research and were not used.

records.name_note: Sources split on which English name leads. NC State's Common Name(s) field stacks seven entries (Common Honey Locust, Honeylocust, Honey Locust, Honey Shucks Locust, Sweet Bean Tree, Sweet Locust, Thorny Locust), in the same order as the page title's parenthetical and led by 'Common Honey Locust'; NC State's Description prose, however, calls the species 'Honey locust' throughout, opening 'Honey locust is a rapidly growing, large deciduous tree in the Fabaceae (bean) family.' MoBot's Common Name field carries the single value 'honey locust.' RHS instead leads with 'thorny locust' in its page title and plant-profile subtitle, listing 'honey locust, sweet locust, three-thorned acacia' under Other common names. MoBot's lead value and NC State's working prose name both give 'honey locust', so 'Honey Locust' is used here; RHS's differing UK-centric lead is disclosed rather than adopted.
unknowns: All data was drawn from the straight-species pages for Gleditsia triacanthos (NC State, MoBot, RHS), each confirmed by URL slug/title match, not from the thornless var. inermis or cultivar pages (Shademaster, Sunburst, Skyline, Skycole) that dominate general search results for this genus.

Thorn length is reported inconsistently: NC State and MoBot both say thorns are 'up to 3 inches long' (solitary or three-branched), while RHS describes spines 'up to 15cm long' (~6 in); both figures are reproduced as stated rather than reconciled.

day_f_min/max and night_f_min/max are left null: this is an outdoor landscape/street tree, and no admissible source frames its cold or heat tolerance in day/night temperature terms (only USDA hardiness zones — NC State 3a-8b, RHS H6 — and general drought/wind/salt/pollution tolerance are given).

If ingested, it is likely to cause death in livestock and pets.  Gasping, weakness, excitement, pupil dilation, spasms, convulsions, coma, respiratory failure." and "The leaves, fruits and seeds contain cyanide compounds, which are poisonous. If a couple of pits are accidentally swallowed, it will not cause poisoning. The pits are more poisonous if they are broken to expose the seeds. Fruits contain cyanogenic compounds, which when acted upon by digestive enzymes, can cause poisoning." Poison Toxic Principle: Cyanogenic glycosides (amygdalin & prunasin). Causes Contact Dermatitis: No. Poison Part (full list): Fruits, Leaves, Seeds. Separately from the human-scoped Poison block, NC State's Problems tags co-list Frequent Disease Problems, Frequent Insect Problems, Messy, Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Children, Problem for Dogs, and Problem for Horses -- toxic_to_pets=true rests specifically on the Problem for Cats and Problem for Dogs tags; the co-listed Problem for Horses tag is livestock-scoped and does not itself support the cat/dog determination. Cedar Waxwings can digest the fruits without releasing the cyanide, but humans are advised not to consume the fruits.' — the same page separately tags Fruit Value To Gardener: Edible, so NC State is internally mixed on edibility and both readings are reported here.

records.name_note: Sources split on which common name leads. NC State's page title parenthetical and its Common Name(s) field both list three entries -- Green Hawthorn, Southern Hawthorn, Washington Hawthorn -- in alphabetical order, and the field's first entry matches the first name in the page title; NC State's description prose then uses 'Green Hawthorn' throughout ('Green hawthorn, like most hawthorns, has gray, thorny bark, bears white flowers in the spring, and produces red fruit in the fall.'; 'Green Hawthorn is a dense, rounded tree that typically grows 20-35' tall with a broad spreading crown.'). Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder page for the species carries a single Common Name field reading 'green hawthorn'. 'Washington Hawthorn' is not species-distinguishing for C. viridis: NC State's separate page for Crataegus phaenopyrum lists Hawthorn, Thornapple and Washington Hawthorn as that species' Common Name(s). RHS's page for the plain species (rhs.org.uk/plants/312999/crataegus-viridis) carries no common name at all. 'Green Hawthorn' is used as common_name on the strength of MoBot's single-value Common Name field plus NC State's leading list entry and body-prose usage.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension's Tags list for Crataegus viridis carries '#non-toxic for cats', '#non-toxic for horses' and '#non-toxic for dogs'. The page has no Poison block (no Poison Severity, Poison Symptoms, Poison Toxic Principle or Poison Part fields, and its Plant Type list -- Native Plant, Perennial, Shrub, Tree -- does not carry 'Poisonous'), so no symptom list, toxic principle or poison-part list is available for this species. On edibility the sources agree rather than disagree, and both hedge: NC State's Edibility field reads 'Fruit is edible, but not of high quality. It can be used to make jelly, but is often left for the birds.', and MoBot's profile says 'Fruits are technically edible, but are usually best left for the birds.' Both sources also flag a physical rather than chemical hazard: NC State tags the plant '#spines' and lists 'Appendage: Thorns' ('When present, thorns grow to 1 1/2 inches long'), and MoBot lists 'Other: Winter Interest, Thorns'.
unknowns: chill_damage_f, cool_rest_note, day_f_min/max, night_f_min/max, humidity_need/pct fields, light_fc_min/good, direct_sun_hours_max, all fertilize_* fields, water_regime, water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, and water_growing_days_est/water_dormant_days_est are left null: no admissible source (NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox, Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder, or RHS) states a numeric damage-onset temperature, dormancy guidance, humidity requirement, foot-candle light value, species-specific direct-sun-hour figure, fertilizer schedule, or a watering statement framed as a dry-down/interval regime for this in-ground landscape tree.

soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are left null: NC State's Soil pH field lists Acid (<6.0), Neutral (6.0-8.0), and Alkaline (>8.0) bands together for this species, meaning both the acid and alkaline open-ended bands are supported, so no ceiling or floor can be set from the closed Neutral band; RHS's species page does not include a Soil/pH field to check against in either direction.

water_regime is left null: two structured moisture readings exist (NC State's Soil Drainage field: Good Drainage, Moist, Occasionally Dry; and MoBot's 'Water: Dry to medium' field) but neither is an explicit watering statement, and MoBot's mid/dry-leaning tag does not map cleanly onto any of the four water_regime enum tokens, so it is disclosed here rather than guessed.

The RHS species page (rhs.org.uk/plants/312999/crataegus-viridis/details) confirms Name Status: Correct but carries no plant-profile subtitle common name, no Other common names field, and no Position/Soil/Exposure/Cultivation content for the plain species -- only the 'Winter King' and 'Big Golden Star' cultivar pages carry that detail -- so it could not corroborate or contradict sun-exposure, soil, or toxicity fields for the species itself.

No admissible-source Clemson (hgic.clemson.edu), UF/IFAS (edis.ifas.ufl.edu / ask.ifas.ufl.edu, aside from the 'Winter King' cultivar page ENH373/ST214, which was excluded as cultivar- rather than species-specific), Penn State (extension.psu.edu), Maryland (extension.umd.edu), or UGA CAES Field Report (fieldreport.caes.uga.edu) page dedicated to Crataegus viridis was found, despite searching each domain directly.

NC State's structured 'is often confused with:' module names Crataegus nitida (not the Winter King cultivar, C. phaenopyrum, or C. crus-galli) as a look-alike species for identification purposes; this is a taxonomic-confusion note, not a common-name split, and was not used to support any schema field.

normalizations: 2026-09-05: forty-seventh batch (cruise throttle) -- a third native tree set: Ohio Buckeye, Red Buckeye, Honey Locust, Shagbark Hickory, Black Cherry, and Green Hawthorn. The run stalled on 2026-09-03 when the weekly usage limit refused one research agent and four Opus audits mid-batch (four records flagged UNVERIFIED by the null-verdict guard, nothing landed), and completed on a plain resume two days later (12/12 agents). land_check.py and covered.py ran clean; verify_quotes.py 101/102 reachable quotes before repair, the one MISS being the synthesized NC State Light quote below. Three sun values changed on the sources' own words: both Aesculus drop full_sun (NC State's species-specific scorch warnings -- 'prone to leaf scorch if planted in full sun' for Ohio Buckeye, 'may experience leaf scorch in the heat of summer' for Red Buckeye, whose NC State Light field carries only Partial Shade -- corroborated by MoBot's Culture text, against unconditional full-sun tags from MoBot and RHS, now disclosed), and Black Cherry drops part_shade (MoBot's single reading against NC State's Full-sun-only Light field, its 'requires full sun' prose, and RHS's Full-sun-only Position). Three nulled citation-form fields were restored with their values unchanged: Red Buckeye's scientific_name_accepted (the one-word 'Correct' quote now paired with RHS's H1 binomial), Honey Locust's soil_base (a cherry-picked NC State planting sentence replaced by MoBot's 'Type: Tree' and 'Suggested Use: Street Tree'), and Shagbark Hickory's is_houseplant (a Plant Type tag list that had dropped Woody Plant). Every name_note was replaced with the auditor's corrected wording for the same description classes as b63/b64 -- the invented 'three or more entries' convention (also scrubbed from citation labels), overstated N-of-M leads, RHS title strings called subtitles, and a MoBot tooltip list reconstructed from overlib attribute markup (that citation removed). Three toxicity_detail fields were repaired as trimmed safety fields from the researchers' own recovered prose plus the auditor's verbatim additions: Ohio Buckeye now carries NC State's 'The seeds, leaves and bark are poisonous' against its structured Fruits/Leaves/Stems Poison Part entries, Causes Contact Dermatitis: No, and RHS's referral tail; Black Cherry adds the Plant Type Poisonous tag and NC State's Fruit Description cyanide caveat against its own Edible tag; Green Hawthorn adds both sources' 'best left for the birds' edibility hedge and the thorn hazard both flag. Ohio Buckeye's NC State Light quote 'Full sun (6+ hours) or Partial Shade (2-6 hours)' was an abbreviation with an invented 'or' and now quotes the single rendered value. One common name cased to catalog title case. toxic_to_pets=true on both Aesculus and Black Cherry rests on NC State's Problem for Cats / Problem for Dogs tags (horses disclosed, not counted); Honey Locust and Green Hawthorn are false on explicit non-toxic-for-cats/dogs tags; Shagbark Hickory is null (no cat/dog-scoped source).
